sections.title: Stronger than "can't"
sections.content: Nem szabad is not just "you're not allowed to" — it's a strong prohibition, closer to "you must not." Where nem lehet often describes a circumstance (something just doesn't work out right now) and nem tud describes a missing personal skill, nem szabad names a rule you would be breaking. Tilos, a word you've just met, is the even more official version you see printed on signs.

sections.title: Three kinds of "can't", side by side
rows: I can't drive. (I lack the skill.)
Ma nem lehet vezetni, mert havazik.
You can't drive today, because it's snowing. (the situation)
You must not drive here. (it's against the rules)

items.spanish: A kórházban nem szabad dohányozni, ez szigorú szabály.
items.english: You must not smoke in the hospital — it's a strict rule.

items.spanish: Itt nem szabad parkolni, különben büntetést kapsz.
items.english: You mustn't park here, or you'll get a fine.

sections.content: Never translate nem szabad as a soft "you can't, but it's fine" — in English terms it's much closer to "you must not" or "it is forbidden to." If breaking a rule could get you a büntetés (fine), nem szabad is almost certainly the right word, not nem lehet.
